Public Art & Murals in St. Augustine: 9 Places Around the City

Sculpted fish gather in a playful underwater scene at the St. Augustine Sculpture Garden. Image courtesy of St. Augustine Sculpture Garden Facebook.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 11:24
Instaread

A bronze Spanish conquistador and a giant painted sea turtle don’t sound like neighbors, but that’s St. Augustine. The city’s public art jumps between centuries, subjects, and styles, with historic figures sharing spaces with murals by contemporary artists. Public art in St. Augustine has a little bit of everything, and the contrast is half the fun.

You don’t need to know much about art to appreciate a good public piece. It’s simply there when you happen to pass by, although it might delay your plans by a minute if you stop for a better look.

Andrew Young Crossing

Bronze footprints stretch across Plaza de la Constitución at Andrew Young Crossing, marking the path civil rights leader Andrew Young walked during a 1964 demonstration in St. Augustine. The monument combines those footprints with granite bands inscribed with words such as “FREEDOM,” “NON-VIOLENCE,” “EQUALITY,” and “JUSTICE,” along with quotations from Young and other national civil rights figures.

The design works well for a public-art roundup because the art and the location are inseparable. Young led demonstrators toward the plaza on June 9, 1964, where a white mob attacked the group, beating Young and knocking him unconscious. The monument was unveiled in 2011, nearly five decades after the march, giving visitors a physical reminder of the route and the principles behind it.

Freedom Trail Markers

This is the plaque on the front lawn of Janie Price’s home, from the ACCORD Civil Right Museum. King stayed with Janie Price in the summer of 1964.

Public art in St. Augustine isn’t limited to statues and murals. The ACCORD Freedom Trail uses 31 historic markers to put the city’s civil rights history directly into the streets, with each marker identifying a location tied to a person, protest, or event. The markers fit naturally into a broader look at public art because they function as public installations that ask you to look, read, and connect the physical place with what happened there.

The marker at 31 King Street, for example, is on a masonry wall facing the Plaza de la Constitución and commemorates demonstrations at the former Woolworth store. At 84 Bridge Street, a marker reveals Trinity United Methodist Church as a gathering place for civil rights demonstrators. Other markers extend through Lincolnville, West Augustine, Uptown, and St. Augustine Beach.

The Freedom Trail is self-guided and open outdoors, with a cellphone audio tour available for visitors who want more context. Maps and brochures are available at the St. Augustine/St. Johns County Visitor Information Center, while the markers themselves require no admission fee beyond the walk there.

St. Augustine Sculpture Garden

At Lakeside Sculpture/Veterans Memorial Park in St. Augustine Beach, 15 monumental sculptures turn a lakeside park into an outdoor gallery. Local artist Thomas Glover White first envisioned the sculpture garden in 1994, eventually working with Marianne Lerbs, Harold Locke, Gary Terbrugge, Deborah Olivieri, and Alvin Felch to create the collection. The City of St. Augustine Beach provided space for the project in 2009, and the garden was dedicated in June 2011.

The sculptures take plenty of inspiration from the area, but they aren’t all easy to figure out at first glance. “Sinornis“ blends bird and dinosaur influences, while “American Beach (Bird Beach Bath)“ has a playful take on the beach. “Spirits of Timucua” references Timucua culture, and “Flowering” connects to the flowers that inspired Florida’s name. Lakeside Park is free to visit and open from sunrise to sundown, seven days a week, with parking available at the site.

Father Francisco López Statue

Father Francisco López overlooks Mission Nombre de Dios with the cross at his side.

A bronze priest appears beneath St. Augustine’s towering Great Cross at the National Shrine of Our Lady of La Leche Mission Nombre de Dios, his arms raised as if addressing the people gathered around him. The Father Francisco López Statue was created by Croatian sculptor Ivan Meštrović and dedicated in 1958, giving a modern sculptor’s interpretation to the Spanish priest associated with St. Augustine’s first Catholic Mass.

López served as chaplain to Pedro Menéndez de Avilés and is traditionally identified as the priest who celebrated Mass on September 8, 1565, after the Spanish landing. Meštrović depicts him in priestly vestments, preaching the Gospel, with the bronze figure standing on a polished granite base. The statue is about 11 feet tall and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2012.

Don Pedro Menéndez de Avilés Statue

Menéndez stands with his sword and coat of arms outside City Hall, marking the downtown site with a nod to St. Augustine’s Spanish beginnings.

St. Augustine’s founder has a statue in front of City Hall that came all the way from his hometown in Spain. The bronze figure of Don Pedro Menéndez de Avilés was given to the city by the people of Avilés and dedicated on September 8, 1972, the same date Menéndez founded the city in 1565.

Menéndez holds his hat in one hand and a sword in the other, with his coat of arms displayed on the pedestal. The statue is a replica of one in Avilés, Spain, making the sculpture itself a connection between the two cities. St. Augustine still celebrates Menéndez’s birthday with a wreath-laying ceremony at the statue each February.

You’ll find the statue at 75 King Street, in the public space known as Parque de Menéndez. There’s no admission fee to see it, and you can stop by whenever you’re exploring the area around City Hall.

Lincolnville Mural

The Lincolnville Mural fills Corner Market’s exterior with portraits honoring people connected to St. Augustine’s African American history.

An 81-foot mural on the side of Corner Market at 97 Martin Luther King Avenue turns a Lincolnville wall into a colorful roll call of local history. Created by St. Augustine artist Nancy Christensen and unveiled in February 2025, the mural features more than 50 people connected to the city’s African American history, including Ray Charles, Dr. Robert Hayling, and Rabbi Israel Dresner.

The building has a history that fits right in with the mural. The Corner Market dates to the 1920s and has housed several businesses over the years, including the Lincolnville Public Library. During the Civil Rights Movement, the library was used for nonviolent protest training, and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. also visited the store.

“Our Wild Life” Mural

A bright coastal mural transforms an otherwise ordinary building into a colorful scene of local wildlife, tropical foliage, and St. Augustine’s seaside character.

Right beside the ocean at St. Johns County Ocean Pier, a vibrant mural puts Florida’s wildlife in the company of surfboards and beach life. Created by Jacksonville artist Brook Page in September 2024, “Our Wild Life” features native plants and animals alongside imagery inspired by St. Augustine Beach’s surf culture.

The mural was the first project selected for the planned St. Johns County Public Art Trail, giving the pier a starring role in the county’s growing collection of public art. Page also incorporated community feedback into the design, with funding from the St. Johns Cultural Council, St. Johns County Tourist Development Council, and Live Wildly Foundation. This piece of public art at 350 A1A Beach Boulevard in St. Augustine Beach is easy to check out during a trip to the pier.

“150 Mythical Miles” Mural

A flood protection wall in Davis Shores has become an enormous nautical chart, thanks to local artist Angela Varga and her neighbor and collaborator, Jed Wolf. Their “150 Mythical Miles” mural, which can be found at 81 N. St. Augustine Blvd. on Anastasia Island, traces the coastline from Cumberland Island, Georgia, to New Smyrna, Florida, filling the wall with maritime folklore and some decidedly unusual creatures.

The mural depicts a six-legged Wampus Cat, a ship-swallowing Kraken, a massive wild pig, a giant alligator, and other mythical creatures associated with the stretch of coast. The result turns a practical flood barrier into a colorful piece of neighborhood art, with the creatures giving the nautical-chart concept plenty of personality.

The project also connects to Davis Shores’ history as a waterfront development. Developer D.P. Davis acquired 1,500 acres on the northeastern portion of Anastasia Island in 1925, then launched a massive dredging operation to create the land for his ambitious new community. The mural brings that history into the present, using a modern flood-protection project as a canvas for a playful map of the same coastal region.

St. Augustine Beach Civic Association Garage Mural

A sea turtle takes center stage on the St. Augustine Beach Civic Association garage, swimming across a deep blue backdrop near the pier. Photo courtesy of St. Johns Cultural Council Facebook.

A giant sea turtle now swims across the garage door of the St. Augustine Beach Civic Association building near the St. Johns County Pier. Local artists Luke and Lucinda Nehemias completed the mural in September 2025 after being selected through a statewide call for artists organized by the St. Johns Cultural Council, with the final design informed by public feedback.

For Luke Nehemias, the location makes the project especially personal, since he works as a first responder at St. Johns County Fire Rescue Station 7 next door. After graduating from Flagler College in 2006, Luke made St. Augustine his home and has since designed logos for St. Johns County Fire Rescue and painted murals at fire stations. His cousin, professional seaside muralist Lucinda Nehemias, joined him to bring the sea turtle mural at 368 A1A Beach Boulevard to life.

Public Art in St. Augustine: The City Is Showing Off

Public art means something different to everyone, and St. Augustine has pieces that embody the city’s history, community, culture, and connection to the coast. It might commemorate a moment in local history, celebrate a neighborhood, or simply give an artist a very large wall to work with. That range is what makes the city’s public art so exciting to encounter.

There’s also something satisfying about art that belongs to the public in the truest sense of the word. Kids walk past it on the way to the beach, locals see it on their morning commute, and visitors stumble across it between lunch and their next stop. Public art in St. Augustine gets to be enjoyed by whoever happens to be there, no ticket or invitation necessary.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is public art in St. Augustine free to see?

Yes. The public art featured here is free to view, since the pieces are installed in public spaces around St. Augustine and St. Augustine Beach. There’s no admission fee for stopping to see the murals, monuments, sculptures, or Freedom Trail markers.

Are any St. Augustine murals located near restaurants or shops?

Yes. Several murals are close to places where you can grab food, browse local shops, or spend time around town. The Lincolnville Mural sits on Martin Luther King Avenue near the neighborhood’s restaurants and businesses, while the murals around St. Augustine Beach are close to the pier, beach access, and nearby dining spots.

Does St. Augustine have a public art program or art trail?

Yes. Public art in St. Augustine is supported through several local programs and organizations, while St. Johns County has also been developing a Public Art Trail. Our Wild Life at the St. Johns County Ocean Pier was selected as the first project for that planned trail, with later projects adding to the county’s collection.

Can visitors walk between several public art pieces in downtown St. Augustine?

Yes, particularly around the historic downtown area. The Andrew Young Crossing, Freedom Trail markers, and Don Pedro Menéndez de Avilés statue are all located within the downtown area, so they can be worked into a walking outing without needing to drive between each stop.

Are St. Augustine’s murals permanent?

Not necessarily. Murals are public artworks, but their lifespan depends on the building, the materials used, maintenance, and future plans for the property. New murals also continue to appear around St. Augustine and St. Johns County, so the public-art lineup can change over time.
